σ = F/A.title: Normal stress: axial force over area
σ = F/A.about: The average normal stress on a cross-section is the force perpendicular to it divided by its area. Tension is positive, compression negative. It is the first check on any rod, bolt, cable or column.
assumptions: The force acts along the member's centroidal axis, so the stress is uniform across the section (no bending)
The section is far from holes, notches, fillets and the point of load application (Saint-Venant); near them use a stress concentration factor K_{t}
A is the original area for engineering stress; true stress uses the current, necked area
Slender members in compression may buckle long before σ reaches the yield strength
A is the area perpendicular to the force, not a side face; use the net area through a hole
vars: internal axial force at the section
related: average shear stress on a section
peak stress at a hole or fillet

example.problem: A steel rod 12 mm in diameter carries a tensile load of 20 kN. Find the normal stress.

τ = V/A.title: Average shear stress: shear force over area
τ = V/A.about: When a force slides one part of a member past another, the shear force on the plane divided by its area gives the average shear stress. It is the standard check for bolts, pins, rivets, keys and glued joints.
assumptions: The shear is spread evenly over the area; the real distribution is not uniform (in a beam it peaks at the neutral axis)
Count every shear plane: a pin in double shear carries V = F/2 on each of two areas
Bending of the pin or bolt is neglected, which is fine for short, snug connections
vars: average shear stress on the plane
shear force acting along the plane
related: bearing stress of a pin of diameter d on a plate of thickness t
peak shear in a rectangular beam
shear stress and strain, while elastic

example.problem: A 10 mm diameter pin in double shear joins a clevis carrying 15 kN. Find the average shear stress in the pin.
steps: Two shear planes, so V = 15 kN/2 = 7.5 kN on each

ε = ΔL/L.title: Normal strain: change in length over original length
ε = ΔL/L.about: Normal strain measures how much a line element stretches per unit length. It is dimensionless and usually small, so it is often quoted in microstrain (με = 10^{−6}) or percent.
assumptions: The deformation is uniform along L; otherwise this is the average strain and the local strain is dε = d(ΔL)/dL
Engineering strain uses the original length; for large stretches the true strain is ln(L/L_{0})
Small strain: ε ≪ 1 so that geometry changes do not matter
related: the sideways strain that comes with it

example.problem: A 2.5 m steel tie stretches 1.8 mm under load. Find the strain.

γ = Δx/h.title: Shear strain: sideways slide over height
γ = Δx/h.about: Shear strain is the change, in radians, of an angle that was originally 90°. For a block whose top slides Δx over its bottom across a height h, the angle is tan γ = Δx/h ≈ γ when small.
assumptions: Small angles: tan γ ≈ γ, good to better than 1% for γ below about 0.17 rad (10°)
The slide varies linearly through the height (uniform shear)
Engineering shear strain γ is twice the tensor shear strain ε_{xy}
vars: shear strain, change in a right angle
relative sideways displacement of the top face
related: shear strain in a twisted shaft

example.problem: A rubber bearing pad 40 mm thick has its top displaced 3 mm sideways relative to its base. Find the shear strain.
steps: γ = 0.075 rad (about 4.3°), small enough for the linear form

t_{i} = σ_{ij} n_{j}.title: Cauchy's formula: traction on any plane
t_{i} = σ_{ij} n_{j}.about: The stress tensor gives the force per unit area (traction) on any plane through a point: multiply it by the plane's unit normal. The traction's component along n is the normal stress on the plane and the rest is shear.
assumptions: n is a unit vector (|n| = 1), pointing out of the material on the side being considered
σ is the stress at the point, so the result is the traction at that point only
Index notation: the repeated j is summed over 1, 2, 3
vars: traction vector, force per area on the plane

example.problem: In plane stress σ_{x} = 80 MPa, σ_{y} = 20 MPa, τ_{xy} = 30 MPa. Find the traction and normal stress on the plane with n = (1, 1)/√2.

σ_{ij} = σ_{ji}.title: Symmetry of the stress tensor
σ_{ij} = σ_{ji}.about: Balancing moments on a tiny cube shows the shear stresses on perpendicular faces must be equal: τ_{xy} = τ_{yx}, and so on. So the 3 × 3 stress tensor has only six independent components, not nine.
assumptions: No body couples or couple stresses (true for ordinary materials; polar or Cosserat media are the exception)
Follows from conservation of angular momentum on an infinitesimal element
vars: Cauchy stress component on the face normal to i, acting in direction j
related: the same statement in engineering notation

example.problem: A shaft surface element has a shear stress of 45 MPa acting along the shaft on the face cut perpendicular to the axis. What shear acts on the longitudinal face?
steps: Moment balance about the element's corner: τ_{xy}(dy dz)dx = τ_{yx}(dx dz)dy
So τ_{yx} = τ_{xy} = 45 MPa: the same shear acts along the longitudinal face, which is why wood shafts split lengthwise

ε_{ij} = (1/2)(∂u_{i}/∂x_{j} + ∂u_{j}/∂x.title: Small-strain tensor from displacements
ε_{ij} = (1/2)(∂u_{i}/∂x_{j} + ∂u_{j}/∂x.about: The strain tensor is the symmetric part of the displacement gradient. Its diagonal terms are the normal strains and its off-diagonal terms are half the engineering shear strains. The antisymmetric part is a rigid rotation and causes no strain.
assumptions: Displacement gradients are small (|∂u_{i}/∂x_{j}| ≪ 1), so products of gradients are dropped
For large deformation use the Green–Lagrange strain E_{ij} = (1/2)(u_{i,j} + u_{j,i} + u_{k,i}u_{k,j})
The displacement field is continuous and differentiable

example.problem: A displacement field is u = 0.002x + 0.001y, v = 0.003y (x, y in m). Find ε_{x}, ε_{y} and γ_{xy}.

p = −σ_{kk}/3.title: Mean (hydrostatic) pressure from the stress tensor
p = −σ_{kk}/3.about: The pressure is minus the average of the three normal stresses. It is the part of the stress that changes volume but not shape, and it is the same in every coordinate system because σ_{kk} is an invariant.
assumptions: Sign convention: tension positive in σ, so compression gives positive p
Repeated index k is summed: σ_{kk} = σ_{11} + σ_{22} + σ_{33}
vars: trace of the stress tensor, the first invariant I_{1}
related: pressure from volume change, bulk modulus K

example.problem: A point has σ_{x} = −50 MPa, σ_{y} = −30 MPa, σ_{z} = −10 MPa. Find the mean pressure.

s_{ij} = σ_{ij} − (σ_{kk}/3) δ_{ij}.title: Deviatoric stress: stress minus its hydrostatic part
s_{ij} = σ_{ij} − (σ_{kk}/3) δ_{ij}.about: Subtracting the mean normal stress from each diagonal term leaves the deviatoric stress, which changes shape but not volume. Metals yield on the deviatoric part alone, which is why von Mises is written in terms of it.
assumptions: Only the diagonal terms change (δ_{ij} = 1 when i = j); shear terms are unchanged
The deviator's trace is always zero: s_{kk} = 0
vars: trace of stress, σ_{11} + σ_{22} + σ_{33}

example.problem: Principal stresses are 120, 40 and −10 MPa. Find the deviatoric principal stresses.

ΔV/V = ε_{kk}.title: Dilatation: volume change from strain
ΔV/V = ε_{kk}.about: For small strains, the fractional change in volume equals the sum of the three normal strains (the trace of the strain tensor). Shear strains change shape but not volume.
assumptions: Small strains: products like ε_{x}ε_{y} are neglected; exactly, V/V_{0} = (1 + ε_{1})(1 + ε_{2})(1 + ε_{3})
Repeated index k summed: ε_{kk} = ε_{x} + ε_{y} + ε_{z}
related: volume change under pressure p, bulk modulus K

example.problem: An aluminium bar (E = 70 GPa, ν = 0.33) carries a uniaxial stress of 140 MPa. Find its fractional volume change.

σ_{x′} = (σ_{x} + σ_{y})/2 + ((σ_{x} − σ.title: Stress transformation: normal stress on a rotated plane
σ_{x′} = (σ_{x} + σ_{y})/2 + ((σ_{x} − σ.about: Gives the normal stress on a plane whose normal is rotated by θ from the x axis, in plane stress. Use it to find the stress across a weld, a grain or a glued seam at an angle.
assumptions: Plane stress: σ_{z} = τ_{xz} = τ_{yz} = 0
θ is measured counter-clockwise from x to x′
Tension positive; τ_{xy} positive on the +x face in the +y direction
Holds for any material: it is just equilibrium, not a material law
vars: normal stress on the rotated face
normal stresses in the original axes
shear stress in the original axes
related: the shear on the same plane

example.problem: At a point σ_{x} = 80 MPa, σ_{y} = −40 MPa, τ_{xy} = 30 MPa. Find the normal stress on a weld at θ = 30°.

τ_{x′y′} = −((σ_{x} − σ_{y})/2) sin(2θ).title: Stress transformation: shear stress on a rotated plane
τ_{x′y′} = −((σ_{x} − σ_{y})/2) sin(2θ).about: Gives the shear stress on a plane rotated by θ in plane stress. It is zero on the principal planes and largest 45° away from them.
assumptions: Plane stress: σ_{z} = τ_{xz} = τ_{yz} = 0
θ counter-clockwise from x; same sign conventions as the normal-stress transformation
vars: shear stress on the rotated face
normal stresses in the original axes
shear stress in the original axes
related: normal stress on the same plane

example.problem: With σ_{x} = 80 MPa, σ_{y} = −40 MPa, τ_{xy} = 30 MPa, find the shear along a weld at θ = 30°.

σ_{1,2} = (σ_{x} + σ_{y})/2 ± √(((σ_{x}.title: Principal stresses in plane stress
σ_{1,2} = (σ_{x} + σ_{y})/2 ± √(((σ_{x}.about: The largest and smallest normal stresses at a point, found on planes with no shear. This is the centre plus or minus the radius of Mohr's circle, and it is what failure theories need.
assumptions: Plane stress, so the third principal stress is σ_{z} = 0; include it when ranking σ_{1} ≥ σ_{2} ≥ σ_{3} for Tresca
Linear elastic or not, it is pure equilibrium and holds for any material
vars: in-plane principal stresses (+ root gives σ_{1})

example.problem: Find the principal stresses for σ_{x} = 80 MPa, σ_{y} = −40 MPa, τ_{xy} = 30 MPa.

τ_{max} = √(((σ_{x} − σ_{y})/2)^{2} + τ_.title: Maximum in-plane shear stress
τ_{max} = √(((σ_{x} − σ_{y})/2)^{2} + τ_.about: The largest shear stress on any plane in the x–y plane, equal to the radius of Mohr's circle. It acts on planes 45° from the principal planes, where the normal stress is the average (σ_{x} + σ_{y})/2.
assumptions: Plane stress
This is the in-plane maximum only; if σ_{1} and σ_{2} have the same sign, the absolute maximum shear is σ_{1}/2 (out of plane, using σ_{3} = 0)

example.problem: A shaft surface has σ_{x} = 60 MPa (bending) and τ_{xy} = 40 MPa (torsion), σ_{y} = 0. Find the maximum in-plane shear.

tan(2θ_{p}) = 2τ_{xy}/(σ_{x} − σ_{y}).title: Principal angle: orientation of the principal planes
tan(2θ_{p}) = 2τ_{xy}/(σ_{x} − σ_{y}).about: Gives the rotation that removes the shear stress. The equation has two solutions 90° apart, one for σ_{1} and one for σ_{2}; substitute back into the transformation formula to tell which is which.
assumptions: Plane stress; θ_{p} counter-clockwise from x
Use atan2(2τ_{xy}, σ_{x} − σ_{y})/2 to get the angle to σ_{1} directly and avoid the quadrant ambiguity
If σ_{x} = σ_{y} and τ_{xy} ≠ 0, θ_{p} = ±45°
vars: angle from x to a principal plane's normal
related: planes of maximum shear, θ_{s} = θ_{p} ± 45°

example.problem: For σ_{x} = 80 MPa, σ_{y} = −40 MPa, τ_{xy} = 30 MPa, find the principal angle.

σ_{v} = √(((σ_{1} − σ_{2})^{2} + (σ_{2}.title: Von Mises equivalent stress
σ_{v} = √(((σ_{1} − σ_{2})^{2} + (σ_{2}.about: Collapses a 3D stress state into one number to compare with the uniaxial yield strength: yield is predicted when σ_{v} ≥ S_{y}. It is based on distortion energy and is the standard criterion for ductile metals.
assumptions: Ductile, isotropic material that yields on shear (distortion), not on hydrostatic pressure
Not for brittle materials (cast iron, concrete, ceramics); use maximum normal stress or Mohr–Coulomb
Static loading; fatigue needs alternating and mean components treated separately
related: one normal and one shear stress

example.problem: Principal stresses are 120, 40 and −30 MPa in a steel with S_{y} = 250 MPa. Find σ_{v} and the safety factor.

σ_{v} = √(σ^{2} + 3τ^{2}).title: Von Mises stress for combined normal and shear stress
σ_{v} = √(σ^{2} + 3τ^{2}).about: The von Mises stress when a point carries one normal stress and one shear stress, as on the surface of a shaft in bending and torsion. Compare it with the yield strength.
assumptions: Plane stress with σ_{y} = 0: only σ_{x} = σ and τ_{xy} = τ
Ductile, isotropic material
Pure shear (σ = 0) gives σ_{v} = √3 τ, so shear yield is S_{sy} = 0.577 S_{y}
related: bending stress at a solid shaft's surface
torsional shear at a solid shaft's surface
Tresca's equivalent for the same state

example.problem: A shaft surface carries σ = 90 MPa from bending and τ = 50 MPa from torsion. Find the von Mises stress.

τ_{max} = (σ_{1} − σ_{3})/2.title: Tresca: maximum shear stress criterion
τ_{max} = (σ_{1} − σ_{3})/2.about: The largest shear stress at a point is half the difference of the largest and smallest principal stresses. Tresca predicts yield when it reaches S_{y}/2. It is simpler and slightly more conservative than von Mises.
assumptions: Principal stresses ordered σ_{1} ≥ σ_{2} ≥ σ_{3}, including the zero out-of-plane stress in plane stress
Ductile, isotropic material
Gives up to about 15% lower allowable than von Mises (worst in pure shear)

example.problem: Principal stresses are 120, 40 and −30 MPa in a steel with S_{y} = 250 MPa. Find τ_{max} and the Tresca safety factor.

σ = E ε.title: Hooke's law in one dimension
σ = E ε.about: In the elastic range, stress is proportional to strain and the constant is Young's modulus E. It is the slope of the straight first part of a stress–strain curve.
assumptions: Linear elastic: below the proportional limit (about the yield strength for most steels)
Uniaxial stress only; with stresses in other directions use the 3D form with ν
Isotropic, homogeneous material; temperature constant (or add αΔT)

example.problem: A strain gauge on a steel member (E = 200 GPa) reads 600 με. Find the stress.

τ = G γ.title: Hooke's law in shear
τ = G γ.about: In the elastic range, shear stress is proportional to shear strain, with the shear modulus G as the constant. Used for shafts in torsion, rubber mounts and adhesive layers.
assumptions: Linear elastic, isotropic material
γ is the engineering shear strain in radians (the change in a right angle), small
γ_{eng} = 2ε_{xy}; using the tensor strain halves τ

example.problem: A neoprene pad (G = 0.9 MPa) has a shear strain of 0.075. Find the shear stress.

ν = −ε_{lat}/ε_{axial}.title: Poisson's ratio
ν = −ε_{lat}/ε_{axial}.about: A bar stretched along its axis gets thinner sideways. Poisson's ratio is the ratio of the sideways strain to the axial strain, with a minus sign so it comes out positive for ordinary materials.
assumptions: Uniaxial stress, linear elastic, isotropic
0 ≤ ν ≤ 0.5 for isotropic materials; 0.5 means incompressible (rubber ≈ 0.49), metals ≈ 0.3, cork ≈ 0

example.problem: In a tensile test, a 12.5 mm diameter aluminium specimen has an axial strain of 0.0024 and its diameter shrinks by 0.0099 mm. Find ν.

ε_{x} = (σ_{x} − ν(σ_{y} + σ_{z}))/E + α.title: Generalised Hooke's law with thermal strain
ε_{x} = (σ_{x} − ν(σ_{y} + σ_{z}))/E + α.about: The strain in x from all three normal stresses and a temperature change. A stress in y or z squeezes x through Poisson's effect; heating adds a free expansion αΔT. The y and z versions follow by cycling the letters.
assumptions: Linear elastic, isotropic material
Small strains; E, ν and α constant over the temperature range
Normal strains do not depend on shear stresses (true for isotropic materials)

example.problem: A steel plate (E = 200 GPa, ν = 0.3, α = 12 × 10^{−6}/K) has σ_{x} = 100 MPa, σ_{y} = 50 MPa, σ_{z} = 0, and is heated 20 K. Find ε_{x}.

γ_{xy} = τ_{xy}/G.title: Shear strain from shear stress (3D Hooke's law)
γ_{xy} = τ_{xy}/G.about: In an isotropic material each shear strain depends only on its own shear stress. The same holds for γ_{yz} and γ_{zx}. Shear does not change the normal strains, and normal stresses do not cause shear strain.
assumptions: Linear elastic, isotropic material (anisotropic materials such as composites couple shear and normal terms)
γ_{xy} is the engineering shear strain, twice the tensor component ε_{xy}
vars: engineering shear strain in the x–y plane

example.problem: An aluminium element (G = 26 GPa) carries τ_{xy} = 52 MPa. Find the shear strain.

σ_{ij} = λ ε_{kk} δ_{ij} + 2μ ε_{ij}.title: Hooke's law in Lamé form
σ_{ij} = λ ε_{kk} δ_{ij} + 2μ ε_{ij}.about: Gives every stress component from the strain tensor in one line. The λ term is a pressure from volume change (diagonal only); the 2μ term follows each strain component. Handy in index-notation derivations and finite elements.
assumptions: Linear elastic, isotropic material; small strains
μ is the shear modulus G; λ has no simple physical meaning by itself
ε_{ij} is the tensor strain, so shear: τ_{xy} = 2μ ε_{xy} = G γ_{xy}
vars: Lamé's second constant, the shear modulus G

example.problem: Steel (λ = 115 GPa, μ = 77 GPa) has ε_{x} = 0.001, ε_{y} = ε_{z} = 0 (uniaxial strain, as in a confined layer). Find σ_{x} and σ_{y}.

G = E/(2(1 + ν)).title: Shear modulus from Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio
G = E/(2(1 + ν)).about: For an isotropic material only two elastic constants are independent. Pure shear is equivalent to tension and compression at 45°, and working that through Hooke's law ties G to E and ν. Given E and ν, this gives the shear modulus G (also called μ) used in torsion and shear problems. Since 0 < ν < 0.5, G lies between E/3 and E/2.
assumptions: Isotropic, linear elastic material; not valid for wood, composites or single crystals
A G outside E/3 to E/2 means a data or unit error

example.problem: Find G for steel with E = 200 GPa and ν = 0.3.

K = E/(3(1 − 2ν)).title: Bulk modulus from Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio
K = E/(3(1 − 2ν)).about: The bulk modulus relates a uniform pressure to the volume change it causes: p = −K ΔV/V. It blows up as ν → 0.5, which is why rubber is nearly incompressible though easy to stretch.
assumptions: Isotropic, linear elastic material
Valid for −1 < ν < 0.5; at ν = 0.5 the material is incompressible (K → ∞)

example.problem: Find the bulk modulus of aluminium (E = 70 GPa, ν = 0.33), and the volume change of a block at 100 MPa of pressure.

λ = Eν/((1 + ν)(1 − 2ν)).title: Lamé's first constant from E and ν
λ = Eν/((1 + ν)(1 − 2ν)).about: Converts the engineering constants E and ν into λ, the constant multiplying volumetric strain in the Lamé form of Hooke's law. Together with μ = G it fully describes an isotropic elastic material. The (1 − 2ν) factor blows up as ν → 0.5, the incompressible limit.
assumptions: Isotropic, linear elastic material
ν < 0.5 (λ → ∞ for an incompressible material)
λ is not the same as the plane-stress constant; for plane stress use λ* = 2λμ/(λ + 2μ)

example.problem: Find λ for steel with E = 200 GPa and ν = 0.3.

τ = μ du/dy.title: Newton's law of viscosity
τ = μ du/dy.about: In a Newtonian fluid, the shear stress between layers is proportional to how fast the velocity changes across them. The constant is the dynamic viscosity μ. Use it for lubricating films, Couette flow and wall shear.
assumptions: Newtonian fluid: μ does not depend on shear rate (water, air, oils; not paint, blood or ketchup)
Laminar, parallel (shear) flow with u along x varying only with y
μ depends strongly on temperature, so use the value at the operating temperature
vars: velocity gradient across the flow (shear rate)
related: linear profile between a moving plate and a fixed one (Couette)

example.problem: A plate slides at 2 m/s over a 0.5 mm film of SAE 30 oil (μ = 0.29 Pa·s). Find the shear stress and the drag on a 0.1 m^{2} plate.

σ_{ij} = −p δ_{ij} + 2μ e_{ij}.title: Stress in an incompressible Newtonian fluid
σ_{ij} = −p δ_{ij} + 2μ e_{ij}.about: The fluid's stress is a pressure acting equally in every direction plus a viscous stress proportional to the strain rate. Putting this into Cauchy's equation of motion gives the Navier–Stokes equations.
assumptions: Newtonian fluid with constant viscosity
Incompressible: e_{kk} = ∇ · v = 0 (otherwise a bulk-viscosity term λ e_{kk} δ_{ij} appears)
Isotropic fluid

example.problem: Water (μ = 1.0 × 10^{−3} Pa·s) at p = 200 kPa flows with u = 500y (1/s), v = 0. Find σ_{xx} and σ_{xy}.

a · b = a_{i} b_{i}.title: Summation convention: the dot product
a · b = a_{i} b_{i}.about: In index notation a repeated index is summed over 1, 2, 3, so a_{i}b_{i} = a_{1}b_{1} + a_{2}b_{2} + a_{3}b_{3}. This short-hand (Einstein's) makes tensor equations compact.
assumptions: Cartesian coordinates with orthonormal basis vectors
An index may appear at most twice in a term: a_{i}b_{i}c_{i} is meaningless
A repeated (dummy) index is summed, a single (free) index means one equation per value
vars: Cartesian components of vectors a and b

example.problem: Find a · b for a = (2, −1, 3) and b = (4, 5, 1).

δ_{ij} a_{j} = a_{i}.title: Kronecker delta: the substitution rule
δ_{ij} a_{j} = a_{i}.about: δ_{ij} is 1 when i = j and 0 otherwise; it is the identity matrix in index form. In the sum over j only the j = i term survives, so multiplying by δ_{ij} and summing simply renames j to i.
assumptions: Cartesian coordinates
δ_{ii} = 3 in three dimensions (the trace of the identity)
vars: Kronecker delta: 1 if i = j, 0 if i ≠ j
related: the same rule on a tensor

example.problem: Evaluate δ_{ij} σ_{ij} for a stress tensor with σ_{11} = 50, σ_{22} = 20, σ_{33} = −10 MPa.
steps: δ_{ij} σ_{ij} = σ_{ii} (only i = j survives)

(a × b)_{i} = ε_{ijk} a_{j} b_{k}.title: Cross product with the permutation symbol
(a × b)_{i} = ε_{ijk} a_{j} b_{k}.about: The permutation (Levi-Civita) symbol ε_{ijk} is +1 for an even ordering of 1, 2, 3, −1 for an odd one and 0 if any index repeats. It writes the cross product, curl and determinant in index notation.
assumptions: Right-handed Cartesian coordinates
related: ε_{ijk} ε_{imn} = δ_{jm} δ_{kn} − δ_{jn} δ_{km}

example.problem: Find the moment r × F for r = (2, 0, 0) m and F = (0, 3, 4) N.

ε_{ijk} ε_{imn} = δ_{jm} δ_{kn} − δ_{jn}.title: The ε–δ identity
ε_{ijk} ε_{imn} = δ_{jm} δ_{kn} − δ_{jn}.about: Contracting two permutation symbols on one index gives a combination of Kronecker deltas. It is the workhorse for proving vector identities like the BAC–CAB rule and ∇ × (∇ × v) = ∇(∇ · v) − ∇^{2}v.
assumptions: Three-dimensional Cartesian coordinates
The shared index must be in the same position in both symbols (cycle indices first if not)
related: a × (b × c) = b(a · c) − c(a · b)

example.problem: Use the identity to simplify [a × (b × c)]_{i}.
steps: [a × (b × c)]_{i} = ε_{ijk} a_{j} ε_{kmn} b_{m} c_{n} = ε_{kij} ε_{kmn} a_{j} b_{m} c_{n}
= (δ_{im} δ_{jn} − δ_{in} δ_{jm}) a_{j} b_{m} c_{n}
example.answer: a × (b × c) = b(a · c) − c(a · b)

σ′_{ij} = Q_{ik} Q_{jl} σ_{kl}.title: Rotating a second-order tensor
σ′_{ij} = Q_{ik} Q_{jl} σ_{kl}.about: Gives the components of stress (or strain) in a rotated coordinate system. Q is the rotation matrix whose rows are the new axes written in the old ones. In matrix form, σ′ = Q σ Q^{T}.
assumptions: Q is orthogonal: Q Q^{T} = I, det Q = +1 for a proper rotation
Q_{ij} = e′_{i} · e_{j}, the cosine of the angle between new axis i and old axis j
Vectors rotate as v′_{i} = Q_{ij} v_{j}
vars: direction cosines, new axis i on old axis j
related: Q = [[cos θ, sin θ], [−sin θ, cos θ]]

example.problem: Rotate σ = [[80, 30], [30, −40]] MPa by θ = 30° and find σ′_{11}.

σ′_{ij} = Q_{ik} Q_{jl} σ_{kl}.try: cos(30 deg)^2 * 80 + 2 cos(30 deg) sin(30 deg) * 30 + sin(30 deg)^2 * (-40)

∫_{S} T_{ij} n_{j} dS = ∫_{V} ∂T_{ij}/∂x.title: Divergence theorem in index form
∫_{S} T_{ij} n_{j} dS = ∫_{V} ∂T_{ij}/∂x.about: The flux of a tensor field out of a closed surface equals the integral of its divergence over the enclosed volume. Applied to stress it turns the total surface force on a body into a volume integral, which leads to the equilibrium equations.
assumptions: S is a closed, piecewise smooth surface bounding V, with n the outward unit normal
T_{ij} is continuously differentiable inside V
Works for a field of any order: for a vector, ∫_{S} v_{j} n_{j} dS = ∫_{V} ∂v_{j}/∂x_{j} dV

example.problem: Check the theorem for v = (x, y, z) on a sphere of radius R = 2 m.
steps: Surface side: v · n = R on the sphere, so ∮ R dS = R(4πR^{2}) = 4πR^{3}

det(σ − λI) = 0.title: Characteristic equation for principal stresses
det(σ − λI) = 0.about: The principal stresses are the eigenvalues of the stress tensor, and the principal directions its eigenvectors. Expanding the determinant gives the cubic λ^{3} − I_{1}λ^{2} + I_{2}λ − I_{3} = 0.
assumptions: σ is symmetric, so all three roots are real and the principal directions are mutually perpendicular
If a row and column have no shear (for example plane stress), that normal stress is already principal

example.problem: Find the principal stresses of σ = [[80, 30, 0], [30, −40, 0], [0, 0, 20]] MPa.
steps: σ_{z} = 20 MPa has no shear, so it is principal

I_{1} = σ_{kk}.title: First stress invariant
I_{1} = σ_{kk}.about: The trace of the stress tensor, σ_{x} + σ_{y} + σ_{z}. A rotation of axes only mixes normal and shear components, never changes their sum, so I_{1} is the same in every coordinate system and equals σ_{1} + σ_{2} + σ_{3}. Minus a third of it is the mean pressure, which drives volume change.
assumptions: Summation over k = 1, 2, 3
Shear components never enter; only the diagonal counts

example.problem: Find I_{1} for σ_{x} = 80, σ_{y} = −40, σ_{z} = 20 MPa (shears do not matter).

I_{2} = (σ_{ii} σ_{jj} − σ_{ij} σ_{ij})/.title: Second stress invariant
I_{2} = (σ_{ii} σ_{jj} − σ_{ij} σ_{ij})/.about: The coefficient of λ in the characteristic cubic, so like I_{1} it is unchanged by rotating the axes. Written out, I_{2} = σ_{x}σ_{y} + σ_{y}σ_{z} + σ_{z}σ_{x} − τ_{xy}^{2} − τ_{yz}^{2} − τ_{zx}^{2}, and in principal stresses σ_{1}σ_{2} + σ_{2}σ_{3} + σ_{3}σ_{1}. Its deviatoric cousin J_{2} drives yielding in the von Mises criterion.
assumptions: σ symmetric; summation over repeated indices
Subtract the shear squares: they are where most hand errors come from

example.problem: Find I_{2} for σ_{x} = 80, σ_{y} = −40, σ_{z} = 20, τ_{xy} = 30 MPa, other shears zero.

I_{3} = det(σ).title: Third stress invariant
I_{3} = det(σ).about: The determinant of the stress tensor, equal to σ_{1}σ_{2}σ_{3}. A determinant doesn't change under a rotation of axes, so like I_{1} and I_{2} it is the same in every frame. It is the constant term in the characteristic cubic whose roots are the principal stresses.
assumptions: Same in every coordinate system, like I_{1} and I_{2}
Its sign tells you whether an odd number of principal stresses are compressive

steps: Expand along the third row: I_{3} = 20 × (80(−40) − 30^{2})

∂σ_{ij}/∂x_{j} + ρ b_{i} = ρ a_{i}.title: Cauchy's equation of motion (equilibrium)
∂σ_{ij}/∂x_{j} + ρ b_{i} = ρ a_{i}.about: Newton's second law at a point in a continuum: the net force from stress gradients plus the body force equals mass times acceleration. With a = 0 it is the equilibrium equation used in every elasticity problem.
assumptions: Continuum with differentiable stress field
b is body force per unit mass (gravity: b = g)
Holds for any material; combine with a constitutive law to solve

example.problem: A concrete column (ρ = 2400 kg/m^{3}) stands 10 m tall, free at the top. Find the vertical stress at its base from self-weight.
steps: Only σ_{z}(z) with b_{z} = −g: dσ_{z}/dz − ρg = 0
With σ_{z} = 0 at the top, σ_{z} = −ρg h at depth h below it

δ = PL/(AE).title: Elongation of an axially loaded bar
δ = PL/(AE).about: How much a straight bar stretches or shortens under an axial load. Combine σ = P/A with ε = σ/E and δ = εL. For several segments, add each segment's PL/(AE).
assumptions: Linear elastic material, stress below the proportional limit
P, A and E constant along L; otherwise sum segments or integrate δ = ∫ P(x)/(A(x)E) dx
Load applied at the centroid (no bending); compression members must not buckle

example.problem: A 2 m steel rod (E = 200 GPa) 20 mm in diameter carries 50 kN tension. Find its elongation.

δ = PL/(AE).try: 50 kN * 2 m / (pi (20 mm)^2 / 4 * 200 GPa) to mm

k = AE/L.title: Axial stiffness of a bar
k = AE/L.about: A bar loaded along its axis behaves like a spring with stiffness AE/L. This lets you treat bars as springs in series (flexibilities add) or in parallel (stiffnesses add) for indeterminate problems.
assumptions: Linear elastic, uniform bar with constant A and E
Axial load only

example.problem: Find the stiffness of a 1.5 m aluminium rod (E = 70 GPa) with a 200 mm^{2} cross-section.

δ_{T} = αΔT L.title: Free thermal expansion of a bar
δ_{T} = αΔT L.about: A bar free to move grows by αΔT per unit length when heated. With no restraint there is no stress; restrain it and the blocked expansion becomes stress.
assumptions: Bar is free to expand (no restraint)
α constant over the temperature range; uniform temperature along L
ΔT is the same in K and °C; never use absolute temperatures here

example.problem: A 30 m steel rail (α = 12 × 10^{−6}/K) warms from 10 °C to 45 °C. How much would it grow if free?

σ = −EαΔT.title: Thermal stress in a fully restrained bar
σ = −EαΔT.about: If a bar is held between rigid walls and heated, its free expansion is blocked entirely and it carries a compressive stress EαΔT. Cooling gives tension. Note the stress does not depend on length or area.
assumptions: Perfectly rigid supports (any give reduces the stress)
Linear elastic; check the stress against yield and the bar against buckling
Uniform temperature change

example.problem: A steel rail (E = 200 GPa, α = 12 × 10^{−6}/K) is welded continuous and warms 35 K. Find the stress.

Σ δ = 0.title: Compatibility for statically indeterminate members
Σ δ = 0.about: When there are more unknown forces than equilibrium equations, add a geometric condition: the deformations must fit together. For a bar between rigid walls, the total change in length is zero.
assumptions: Rigid supports that do not move (otherwise Σ δ equals the known gap or support movement)
Each deformation is written in terms of the forces with a force–deformation law (δ = PL/(AE) + αΔT L)
Small deformations
vars: deformation of each segment, mechanical plus thermal

example.problem: A 400 mm steel bar (E = 200 GPa, A = 500 mm^{2}) sits between rigid walls. A 60 kN load acts at 100 mm from the left wall. Find the left reaction.
example.answer: R_{L} = 45 kN, R_{R} = 15 kN (the nearer wall takes three quarters)

P_{1} = P k_{1}/(k_{1} + k_{2}).title: Load sharing between two parallel bars
P_{1} = P k_{1}/(k_{1} + k_{2}).about: When two members side by side carry a load through a rigid plate, they stretch the same amount, so each takes load in proportion to its stiffness. The stiffer member takes more.
assumptions: The plate is rigid and the load is placed so it does not tilt
Both members are linear elastic, with k = AE/L
Members start snug (no initial gap or misfit)

example.problem: A concrete pier has a steel rod cast inside. Concrete: A = 0.09 m^{2}, E = 25 GPa. Steel: A = 0.002 m^{2}, E = 200 GPa. Same length. Find the share of a 1 MN load taken by the steel.
steps: Same L, so k ∝ AE: steel 0.002 × 200 = 0.4, concrete 0.09 × 25 = 2.25 (GPa·m^{2})

σ_{h} = pr/t.title: Hoop stress in a thin-walled cylinder
σ_{h} = pr/t.about: Internal pressure tries to split a cylinder lengthwise; the wall resists with a circumferential (hoop) stress. It is twice the axial stress, so pipes and tanks fail along their length.
assumptions: Thin wall: r/t ≥ 10 (stress roughly uniform through the wall); thicker walls need Lamé's thick-wall solution
r is the inner (or mean) radius; p is gauge pressure
Away from end caps, nozzles and supports
Hoop stress is twice the axial stress, which is why pipes split lengthwise

example.problem: A compressed-air tank of inner diameter 600 mm and wall 8 mm holds 1.5 MPa. Find the hoop stress.

σ_{a} = pr/(2t).title: Axial stress in a thin-walled cylinder
σ_{a} = pr/(2t).about: Pressure on the end caps pulls a closed cylinder lengthwise. The force pπr^{2} is carried by the wall ring 2πrt, giving half the hoop stress.
assumptions: Closed ends (open pipes with sliding seals carry no axial pressure stress)
Thin wall, r/t ≥ 10
Away from end caps and discontinuities
p is gauge pressure; use MPa with mm and get MPa

example.problem: For the tank with inner diameter 600 mm, wall 8 mm and pressure 1.5 MPa, find the axial stress.

σ = pr/(2t).title: Wall stress in a thin-walled sphere
σ = pr/(2t).about: A sphere under internal pressure has the same tensile stress in every direction in its wall: half a cylinder's hoop stress. That is why spheres make the lightest pressure vessels.
assumptions: Thin wall, r/t ≥ 10
Uniform internal gauge pressure
Away from openings and supports
vars: membrane stress, equal in all in-plane directions
related: wall needed for an allowable stress

example.problem: A spherical propane tank 2 m in inner diameter holds 1.8 MPa. With an allowable stress of 140 MPa, what wall thickness is needed?
steps: t = 6.43 mm (r/t = 156, thin wall is fine)

τ = Tρ/J.title: Torsion formula: shear stress in a twisted shaft
τ = Tρ/J.about: A torque twists a circular shaft and sets up shear stress on its cross-section. The stress is zero at the centre and grows linearly with distance from it, reaching τ_{max} = Tc/J at the outer surface.
assumptions: The shaft is circular, solid or hollow, and straight, with a constant cross-section along the length considered
The material is homogeneous, isotropic and linear elastic (stress stays below the proportional limit)
Plane cross-sections stay plane and radial lines stay straight as the shaft twists
Small angles of twist
Far enough from where the torque is applied or the diameter changes (Saint-Venant's principle)
vars: internal torque at the section (from a free-body diagram)
radial distance from the shaft's centre, 0 ≤ ρ ≤ c
polar moment of inertia of the cross-section
related: hollow shaft, outer radius c_{o}, inner radius c_{i}
largest stress, at the outer surface
angle of twist over a length L

example.problem: A solid steel shaft 50 mm in diameter carries a torque of 1.5 kN·m. Find the shear stress at its surface and 10 mm from its centre.
steps: At ρ = 10 mm, the stress scales linearly: τ = 61.1 MPa × 10/25 = 24.4 MPa
example.answer: τ_{max} ≈ 61.1 MPa; 24.4 MPa at ρ = 10 mm

τ = Tρ/J.try: 1.5 kN m * 25 mm / (pi (25 mm)^4 / 2) to MPa

τ_{max} = Tc/J.title: Maximum torsional shear stress in a circular shaft
τ_{max} = Tc/J.about: The torsion formula evaluated at the outer surface, where shear stress is largest. This is the number to compare with the allowable shear stress when sizing a shaft.
assumptions: Circular solid or hollow shaft, constant section
Linear elastic, homogeneous, isotropic material
Away from keyways, shoulders and load points (use K_{t} there)
vars: shear stress at the outer surface

example.problem: A hollow steel shaft, 60 mm outside and 40 mm inside diameter, carries 2 kN·m. Find the maximum shear stress.

φ = TL/(GJ).title: Angle of twist of a circular shaft
φ = TL/(GJ).about: How far one end of a shaft rotates relative to the other under torque. Shafts are often sized for stiffness (a limit like 1° per metre) rather than strength.
assumptions: Circular shaft, linear elastic material
T, G and J constant along L; otherwise sum segments: φ = Σ T_{i}L_{i}/(G_{i}J_{i})
Result is in radians
Use J (polar, πd^{4}/32), not I (πd^{4}/64), or the twist comes out twice as large
related: the stress at the same time

example.problem: A solid steel shaft (G = 79 GPa) 40 mm in diameter and 1.2 m long carries 800 N·m. Find the twist.

k_{t} = GJ/L.title: Torsional stiffness of a shaft
k_{t} = GJ/L.about: Torque needed per radian of twist, from φ = TL/(GJ). A shaft acts as a torsional spring: stiffer with a stiffer material (G), a fatter section (J ∝ d^{4}) and a shorter length. Use k_{t} for torsional vibration (ω_{n} = √(k_{t}/I_{rot})) and for indeterminate shafts.
assumptions: Circular, uniform shaft of linear elastic material
Shafts in series: 1/k = Σ 1/k_{i}; side by side (same twist): k = Σ k_{i}
Per radian, not per degree
related: torsional natural frequency with a disc of inertia I

example.problem: Find the torsional stiffness of the 40 mm, 1.2 m steel shaft (G = 79 GPa).

k_{t} = GJ/L.try: 79 GPa * pi * (40 mm)^4 / 32 / 1.2 m to kN m

P = Tω.title: Power transmitted by a rotating shaft
P = Tω.about: Power is torque times angular speed. Use it to get the torque on a motor or gearbox shaft from its rated power and speed, then size the shaft.
assumptions: ω in rad/s: ω = 2πn/60 for n in rpm; using rpm directly is a factor of 9.55 out
Steady rotation; T is the torque carried at that section
Through a gearbox P is (nearly) constant, so a slower shaft carries more torque

example.problem: A motor delivers 15 kW at 1450 rpm. Find the shaft torque.

J = πd^{4}/32.title: Polar moment of inertia of a solid circular shaft
J = πd^{4}/32.about: The geometric property that measures a circular section's resistance to twisting. It goes as d^{4}, so a small increase in diameter stiffens a shaft a lot. Equal to πc^{4}/2 with c = d/2.
assumptions: Solid circular section; for non-circular sections J does not give the torsion constant
J = I_{x} + I_{y} = 2I for a circle

example.problem: Find J for a 50 mm diameter shaft.

J = π(d_{o}^{4} − d_{i}^{4})/32.title: Polar moment of inertia of a hollow circular shaft
J = π(d_{o}^{4} − d_{i}^{4})/32.about: Subtract the bore's J from the outer circle's. Because the material near the centre carries little stress, a hollow shaft saves a lot of weight for a small loss of strength.
assumptions: Concentric circular bore
For a thin tube of mean radius r and wall t, J ≈ 2πr^{3}t
Subtract the fourth powers, not the diameters; /32 for J, /64 for I

example.problem: Compare a solid 50 mm shaft with a hollow one 60 mm OD × 40 mm ID: J and area.
steps: Hollow is 66% stiffer with 20% less material

τ = T/(2t A_{m}).title: Shear stress in a thin-walled closed tube (Bredt)
τ = T/(2t A_{m}).about: In a closed thin-walled section of any shape, torque sets up a constant shear flow q = T/(2A_{m}) around the wall. The stress is largest where the wall is thinnest.
assumptions: Closed section (an open section such as a slit tube is far weaker and needs a different formula)
Thin wall: t small compared with the section size; stress uniform through t
A_{m} is the area enclosed by the wall's mid-line, not the material area
vars: shear stress at a point in the wall
area enclosed by the median line
related: shear flow, constant around the wall

example.problem: A rectangular aluminium tube 100 × 50 mm (to wall mid-lines) with a 3 mm wall carries 1.2 kN·m. Find the shear stress.

τ = T/(2t A_{m}).try: 1.2 kN m / (2 * 3 mm * 100 mm * 50 mm) to MPa

φ = (TL/(4A_{m}^{2} G)) ∮ ds/t.title: Angle of twist of a thin-walled closed tube
φ = (TL/(4A_{m}^{2} G)) ∮ ds/t.about: The twist of a closed thin-walled section of any shape. The integral runs around the wall's mid-line; for constant thickness it is just the perimeter over t.
assumptions: Closed, thin-walled section; linear elastic material
Uniform section along L
For piecewise constant walls, ∮ ds/t = Σ s_{i}/t_{i}
vars: area enclosed by the median line

example.problem: The 100 × 50 mm aluminium tube (t = 3 mm, G = 26 GPa) is 2 m long and carries 1.2 kN·m. Find the twist.

σ = −My/I.title: Flexure formula: bending stress in a beam
σ = −My/I.about: A bending moment puts one side of a beam in tension and the other in compression, with stress varying linearly from zero at the neutral axis. With y up and positive (sagging) M, the top is in compression, hence the minus sign.
assumptions: Straight beam of linear elastic, homogeneous material; plane sections stay plane
Bending about a principal axis of the section, which is symmetric about the load plane
y measured from the neutral axis, which passes through the centroid
Away from load points and supports; small deflections
vars: second moment of area about the neutral axis
related: largest magnitude, at the outer fibre

example.problem: A 50 × 150 mm timber joist (h = 150 mm vertical) carries M = 4 kN·m. Find the stress 50 mm above the neutral axis.

σ = −My/I.try: -4 kN m * 50 mm / (50 mm * (150 mm)^3 / 12) to MPa

σ_{max} = Mc/I = M/S.title: Maximum bending stress and section modulus
σ_{max} = Mc/I = M/S.about: The largest bending stress, at the fibre farthest from the neutral axis. The section modulus S = I/c bundles the geometry into one number; steel tables list it, and sizing is just S ≥ M/σ_{allow}.
assumptions: Same as the flexure formula: linear elastic, plane sections, symmetric section
For unsymmetric sections (T-beams), c differs top and bottom, so check both
Units: N·mm over mm^{3} gives MPa; mixing kN·m with mm^{3} is a factor of 10^{6} out
vars: distance from the neutral axis to the outer fibre

example.problem: The 50 × 150 mm joist carries M = 4 kN·m. Find the maximum bending stress.

σ_{max} = Mc/I = M/S.try: 4 kN m / (50 mm * (150 mm)^2 / 6) to MPa

τ = VQ/(It).title: Transverse shear stress in a beam
τ = VQ/(It).about: Shear force in a beam causes shear stress on horizontal and vertical planes, zero at the top and bottom faces and largest near the neutral axis. Q is the first moment of the area beyond the level where τ is wanted.
assumptions: Linear elastic, prismatic beam; flexure formula valid
τ is averaged across the width t at that level, accurate when t is small compared with depth (less so for wide flat sections)
Not valid at a free edge where shear must vanish (flange tips need shear flow)
vars: shear stress at the level considered
first moment of the area above (or below) that level about the neutral axis, A′ȳ′
second moment of the whole section
width of the section at that level
related: shear flow, for fasteners and welds

example.problem: A 50 × 150 mm rectangular beam carries V = 6 kN. Find τ at 25 mm above the neutral axis.
steps: Area above: 50 × 50 = 2500 mm^{2}, centroid at 50 mm above NA, Q = 125 000 mm^{3}

τ_{max} = 3V/(2A).title: Maximum shear stress in a rectangular beam
τ_{max} = 3V/(2A).about: For a rectangular section the shear stress follows a parabola across the depth and peaks at the neutral axis at 1.5 times the average V/A. Important for short, deep or timber beams.
assumptions: Rectangular cross-section, linear elastic
From τ = VQ/(It) with Q = bh^{2}/8 at the neutral axis
vars: shear stress at the neutral axis
related: I-beam, shear taken by the web

example.problem: A 50 × 150 mm timber beam carries a shear of 6 kN. Find the maximum shear stress.

τ_{max} = 4V/(3A).title: Maximum shear stress in a solid circular beam
τ_{max} = 4V/(3A).about: For a solid round section in bending, transverse shear peaks at the neutral axis at 4/3 of the average. Used for pins, axles and round bars carrying shear.
assumptions: Solid circular cross-section, linear elastic
From τ = VQ/(It) with Q = d^{3}/12 and t = d at the neutral axis
For a thin-walled tube, τ_{max} = 2V/A instead
vars: shear stress at the neutral axis

example.problem: A 20 mm round axle carries a shear of 8 kN. Find the maximum transverse shear stress.

dV/dx = −w.title: Load–shear relation
dV/dx = −w.about: The slope of the shear diagram equals minus the distributed load (load acting downward). Integrating, the change in shear between two points is minus the load area between them. Point loads cause jumps.
assumptions: w is distributed load per length, positive downward
Sign convention: positive shear rotates an element clockwise
At a point load P the shear jumps by −P (downward load)

example.problem: A simply supported 6 m beam carries 5 kN/m. Left reaction 15 kN. Find the shear at x = 4 m.

dM/dx = V.title: Shear–moment relation
dM/dx = V.about: The slope of the bending-moment diagram equals the shear force. So the moment is largest (or smallest) where the shear crosses zero, and the change in moment between two points is the area under the shear diagram.
assumptions: Same sign convention as dV/dx = −w (positive moment sags)
An applied couple causes a jump in M

example.problem: In the 6 m simply supported beam with 5 kN/m (reaction 15 kN), find the maximum moment.
steps: M_{max} = area under V from 0 to 3 = (1/2)(15)(3) = 22.5 kN·m

EI d^{2}v/dx^{2} = M.title: Moment–curvature equation for beam deflection
EI d^{2}v/dx^{2} = M.about: Curvature of the deflected beam is M/(EI). Integrate twice, apply the support conditions, and you get the slope and deflection everywhere.
assumptions: Euler–Bernoulli beam: linear elastic, plane sections, shear deformation neglected (L/h ≳ 10)
Small slopes (curvature ≈ v″)
v measured upward, positive M sags

example.problem: A cantilever of length L has a tip load P (downward). Find the tip deflection by integration. Use L = 2 m, P = 1 kN, EI = 500 kN·m^{2}.
steps: With x from the wall, M = −P(L − x)

EI d^{4}v/dx^{4} = −w.title: Fourth-order beam equation
EI d^{4}v/dx^{4} = −w.about: Combines dV/dx = −w, dM/dx = V and EIv″ = M into one equation. Integrate four times and use four boundary conditions; handy for distributed loads and indeterminate beams.
assumptions: Euler–Bernoulli beam with constant EI
w positive downward, v positive upward
Boundary conditions: fixed v = v′ = 0; pinned v = M = 0; free M = V = 0

example.problem: A simply supported beam (L = 6 m, EI = 20 MN·m^{2}) carries w = 5 kN/m. Find the midspan deflection.
steps: Integrating with v = v″ = 0 at both ends gives v = −(w/(24EI))(x^{4} − 2Lx^{3} + L^{3}x)

P_{cr} = π^{2}EI/(KL)^{2}.title: Euler buckling load of a column
P_{cr} = π^{2}EI/(KL)^{2}.about: A slender column in compression suddenly bows sideways at this load, well below the crushing strength. K is the effective-length factor set by the end conditions; use the smaller I of the section.
assumptions: Perfectly straight, slender, linear elastic column with a centred load
Valid only while σ_{cr} = P_{cr}/A stays below the proportional limit (slenderness KL/r large, roughly > 100 for structural steel); otherwise use Johnson's parabola
K: pinned–pinned 1, fixed–free 2, fixed–pinned 0.7, fixed–fixed 0.5 (design values slightly higher)

example.problem: A pinned–pinned aluminium strut (E = 70 GPa) 1.5 m long is a solid rod 25 mm in diameter. Find the buckling load.
steps: Check: σ = 5888/491 = 12 MPa, well below yield, so Euler applies

I = bh^{3}/12.title: Second moment of area of a rectangle
I = bh^{3}/12.about: Bending stiffness of a rectangular section about its centroidal axis parallel to b. It grows with the cube of depth, which is why joists stand on edge.
assumptions: Axis through the centroid, parallel to the side b
h is measured perpendicular to the bending axis (in the direction of the load)
vars: second moment of area about the centroidal axis

example.problem: Compare a 50 × 150 mm joist on edge and laid flat.

I = πd^{4}/64.title: Second moment of area of a solid circle
I = πd^{4}/64.about: Bending stiffness of a round bar about any diameter. It grows with d^{4} because both the area and its distance from the axis grow with d: doubling the diameter makes a bar 16 times stiffer. It is half the polar moment J, since I_{x} + I_{y} = J.
assumptions: Axis through the centre (any diameter); use the parallel-axis theorem for any other axis
Use the diameter, not the radius: with r it is πr^{4}/4
Don't confuse I (bending, /64) with J (torsion, /32)
vars: second moment of area about a diameter

example.problem: Find I for a 25 mm round steel bar used as a short cantilever pin.

I = π(d_{o}^{4} − d_{i}^{4})/64.title: Second moment of area of a hollow circle (tube)
I = π(d_{o}^{4} − d_{i}^{4})/64.about: Bending stiffness of a round tube: the outer circle minus the bore. Tubes give high stiffness per weight because material sits far from the axis.
assumptions: Concentric bore; axis through the centre
Subtract the fourth powers, not the diameters: (d_{o} − d_{i})^{4} is wrong
Thin tube of mean radius r and wall t: I ≈ πr^{3}t

example.problem: Find I for a steel tube 48.3 mm OD with a 3.2 mm wall (scaffold tube).

I = Ī + Ad^{2}.title: Parallel axis theorem
I = Ī + Ad^{2}.about: Moves a second moment of area from a part's own centroid to any parallel axis. Used to build I for I-beams, T-sections and built-up shapes from rectangles.
assumptions: Ī must be about the part's own centroidal axis
d is the perpendicular distance between the two parallel axes
Only works from the centroid outward; to move between two non-centroidal axes, go through the centroid
vars: second moment about the new axis
second moment about the part's centroidal axis
related: same rule for polar moments and mass moments

example.problem: An I-section has two 100 × 10 mm flanges and a 10 × 180 mm web (overall depth 200 mm). Find I about the centroid.

Cantilever, end load P ‖ PL ‖ PL^{3}/(3E.title: Cantilever with an end load: moment and deflection
Cantilever, end load P ‖ PL ‖ PL^{3}/(3E.about: A beam fixed at one end with a point load P at the free end. The moment is largest at the wall, PL, and the tip deflects PL^{3}/(3EI). A diving board, a shelf bracket or a robot arm.
assumptions: Euler–Bernoulli beam, linear elastic, constant EI
Perfectly fixed support (real connections are less stiff, so deflection is larger)
Small deflections; self-weight neglected unless added separately
related: deflection along the beam, x from the wall

example.problem: A steel cantilever (E = 200 GPa), 1.5 m long, is a 50 × 100 mm solid bar (100 mm deep) with a 2 kN end load. Find M_{max} and the tip deflection.

Cantilever, uniform w ‖ wL^{2}/2 ‖ wL^{4.title: Cantilever with a uniform load: moment and deflection
Cantilever, uniform w ‖ wL^{2}/2 ‖ wL^{4.about: A cantilever carrying a uniform load w over its whole length, such as a balcony slab or the beam's own weight. The wall moment is wL^{2}/2 and the tip deflects wL^{4}/(8EI).
assumptions: Euler–Bernoulli beam, linear elastic, constant EI
Load uniform over the full length; perfectly fixed support
Small deflections

example.problem: A 2 m aluminium cantilever (E = 70 GPa, I = 8 × 10^{6} mm^{4}) carries 1.2 kN/m. Find the wall moment and tip deflection.

Cantilever, end moment M₀ ‖ M_{0} ‖ M_{0.title: Cantilever with an end couple: moment and deflection
Cantilever, end moment M₀ ‖ M_{0} ‖ M_{0.about: A pure couple M_{0} at the free end bends a cantilever into a circular arc. The moment is M_{0} everywhere and the tip deflects M_{0}L^{2}/(2EI).
assumptions: Euler–Bernoulli beam, linear elastic, constant EI
Small deflections (the exact shape is a circular arc of radius EI/M_{0})
Unlike a tip force, the moment does not grow toward the wall: it is M_{0} everywhere

example.problem: A 1 m steel strip (E = 200 GPa, I = 2 × 10^{4} mm^{4}) has a 50 N·m couple at its end. Find the tip deflection.

Simply supported, centre load P ‖ PL/4 ‖.title: Simply supported beam with a centre load
Simply supported, centre load P ‖ PL/4 ‖.about: A beam on two supports with a point load at midspan. Each support takes P/2; the moment peaks at the load at PL/4 and so does the deflection, PL^{3}/(48EI). The classic three-point bend test.
assumptions: Pin and roller supports (free to rotate); Euler–Bernoulli beam, constant EI
Load exactly at midspan; small deflections
related: E from a three-point bend test

example.problem: A 4 m steel beam (E = 200 GPa, I = 8.36 × 10^{6} mm^{4}) carries 10 kN at midspan. Find M_{max} and the deflection.

Simply supported, uniform w ‖ wL^{2}/8 ‖.title: Simply supported beam with a uniform load
Simply supported, uniform w ‖ wL^{2}/8 ‖.about: The most common beam case: floor joists, bridges and shelves. The moment peaks at midspan at wL^{2}/8 and the midspan deflection is 5wL^{4}/(384EI). Deflection limits like L/360 often govern.
assumptions: Pin and roller supports; Euler–Bernoulli beam, constant EI
Load uniform over the whole span; small deflections

example.problem: A timber joist (E = 11 GPa, 50 × 200 mm deep) spans 4 m and carries 2 kN/m. Find M_{max} and the midspan deflection.

Cantilever, end load P ‖ PL^{2}/(2EI).title: End slope of a cantilever with an end load
Cantilever, end load P ‖ PL^{2}/(2EI).about: The rotation of the free end of a cantilever with a point load P at the tip. Needed when something mounted at the tip must stay level, or in superposition.
assumptions: Euler–Bernoulli beam, linear elastic, constant EI, fixed support
Small slopes; result in radians
related: deflection of a rigid extension of length a

example.problem: For the 1.5 m steel cantilever (E = 200 GPa, I = 4.167 × 10^{6} mm^{4}) with a 2 kN end load, find the end slope.

Cantilever, uniform w ‖ wL^{3}/(6EI).title: End slope of a cantilever with a uniform load
Cantilever, uniform w ‖ wL^{3}/(6EI).about: The rotation at the free end of a cantilever carrying a uniform load. The wall holds the root level, and the slope builds up along the beam, so the tip turns the most.
assumptions: Euler–Bernoulli beam, linear elastic, constant EI, fully fixed support
Uniform load over the full length; small slopes
Use consistent units: w in N/m with L in m, I in m^{4}

example.problem: A 2 m aluminium balcony bracket (E = 70 GPa, I = 8 × 10^{6} mm^{4}) carries 1.2 kN/m. Find the end slope.

Simply supported, centre load P ‖ PL^{2}.title: End slope of a simply supported beam with a centre load
Simply supported, centre load P ‖ PL^{2}.about: How far each end of a simply supported beam rotates under a midspan point load. By symmetry the centre stays level and the ends turn equal and opposite. Check it where the beam sits on bearings or fits into other parts.
assumptions: Pin and roller supports, Euler–Bernoulli beam, constant EI
Load at midspan; both ends rotate by the same amount in opposite senses

example.problem: For the 4 m steel beam (E = 200 GPa, I = 8.36 × 10^{6} mm^{4}) with 10 kN at midspan, find the end slope.

Simply supported, uniform w ‖ wL^{3}/(24.title: End slope of a simply supported beam with a uniform load
Simply supported, uniform w ‖ wL^{3}/(24.about: The rotation at each support of a simply supported beam under a uniform load. The ends are free to turn, so they rotate most there while the midspan stays flat by symmetry. It matters at bearings and where a floor joist meets a finished wall.
assumptions: Pin and roller supports, Euler–Bernoulli beam, constant EI
Uniform load over the full span; small slopes
Slope in radians; keep w in N/m and L in m (or N/mm and mm), not a mix

example.problem: A timber joist (E = 11 GPa, I = 3.333 × 10^{7} mm^{4}, a 100 × 200 mm section) spans 4 m under 2 kN/m. Find the end slope.

dp/dz = −ρg.title: Hydrostatic pressure gradient
dp/dz = −ρg.about: In a fluid at rest, pressure increases going down because each layer supports the weight of the fluid above it. Integrate it to get pressure with depth in liquids or with altitude in the atmosphere.
assumptions: Fluid at rest (or moving as a rigid body), so no shear stresses
z points up; g constant
For a liquid ρ is constant; for a gas use ρ = p/(RT) before integrating
related: the general equilibrium equation it comes from

example.problem: Find the pressure drop per metre of height in air at sea level (ρ = 1.225 kg/m^{3}).
steps: About 1 hPa for every 8.3 m of climb

p = p_{0} + ρgh.title: Pressure at a depth in a liquid
p = p_{0} + ρgh.about: Pressure below a free surface grows linearly with depth. It depends only on depth, not the shape of the container. Use p_{0} = atmospheric for absolute pressure or 0 for gauge pressure.
assumptions: Liquid at rest with constant density
h measured down from the surface where p = p_{0}
vars: pressure at the surface (101.3 kPa for atmosphere)

example.problem: Find the absolute pressure on a diver 30 m down in seawater (ρ = 1025 kg/m^{3}).

F_{b} = ρgV.title: Archimedes' principle: buoyant force
F_{b} = ρgV.about: A body immersed in a fluid is pushed up by a force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces. It floats if that can match its weight before it is fully submerged.
assumptions: Fluid at rest with constant density
ρ is the fluid's density and V the displaced (submerged) volume, not the body's
The force acts through the centroid of the displaced volume (centre of buoyancy)

example.problem: A 0.2 m^{3} steel buoy weighs 1200 N. What is the buoyant force when fully submerged in seawater (1025 kg/m^{3}), and does it float?
steps: 2011 N > 1200 N, so it floats with 1200/2011 = 60% submerged

F = p_{c} A.title: Hydrostatic force on a submerged flat plate
F = p_{c} A.about: The total pressure force on a plane surface equals the pressure at its centroid times its area. The force acts lower, at the centre of pressure, because pressure grows with depth.
assumptions: Liquid at rest with constant density
p_{c} = ρgh_{c}, h_{c} the vertical depth of the plate's centroid (gauge, if air is on the other side)
Centre of pressure along the slope: y_{cp} = y_{c} + Ī/(y_{c}A)
vars: resultant pressure force, normal to the plate

example.problem: A vertical sluice gate 2 m wide and 3 m tall has water up to its top edge. Find the force on it and where it acts.
example.answer: F ≈ 88.3 kN, acting 2 m below the surface

p + ρv^{2}/2 + ρgz = constant.title: Bernoulli's equation
p + ρv^{2}/2 + ρgz = constant.about: Along a streamline, pressure, kinetic energy and potential energy per unit volume trade off but their sum stays constant. Use it for flow through nozzles, Venturi meters, tank draining and pitot tubes.
assumptions: Steady flow
Incompressible (gases: Mach < 0.3)
Frictionless (inviscid): no losses; add a head-loss term for real pipes
Along a single streamline (or anywhere in irrotational flow)
No pump or turbine between the two points

example.problem: Water flows at 2 m/s and 200 kPa in a 100 mm pipe that narrows to 50 mm at the same height. Find the pressure in the throat.

Re = ρvD/μ.title: Reynolds number
Re = ρvD/μ.about: The ratio of inertial to viscous forces. In a pipe, flow is laminar below about 2300 and turbulent above about 4000. It decides which friction and heat-transfer correlations apply.
assumptions: D is the characteristic length: pipe diameter, or hydraulic diameter 4A/P for non-circular ducts; plate length for external flow
v is the mean velocity
Transition values depend on geometry: pipe ≈ 2300, flat plate ≈ 5 × 10^{5}

example.problem: Water (ρ = 998 kg/m^{3}, μ = 1.0 × 10^{−3} Pa·s) flows at 1.5 m/s in a 25 mm pipe. Is it laminar?

Q = πR^{4}Δp/(8μL).title: Hagen–Poiseuille flow in a pipe
Q = πR^{4}Δp/(8μL).about: Volume flow rate for fully developed laminar flow in a round pipe. Flow goes as R^{4}, so halving the radius cuts the flow 16-fold at the same pressure drop; vital for blood vessels, capillaries and hydraulics.
assumptions: Laminar flow, Re < 2300 (check after solving)
Steady, incompressible, Newtonian fluid
Fully developed (far from the entrance) in a straight, rigid, circular pipe
No slip at the wall
related: mean speed is half the centreline speed
same result as a Darcy friction factor

example.problem: Oil (μ = 0.1 Pa·s) flows through a 10 mm diameter tube 2 m long under a 50 kPa pressure drop. Find Q.
steps: That is 0.0614 L/s; check v = Q/A = 0.78 m/s, Re = 900·0.78·0.01/0.1 ≈ 70, laminar

Q = πR^{4}Δp/(8μL).try: pi * (5 mm)^4 * 50 kPa / (8 * 0.1 Pa s * 2 m) to L/s

h_{f} = f (L/D) v^{2}/(2g).title: Darcy–Weisbach head loss in a pipe
h_{f} = f (L/D) v^{2}/(2g).about: The friction loss in a pipe, expressed as a height of fluid. Multiply by ρg to get a pressure drop. The friction factor f comes from 64/Re for laminar flow or the Moody chart (Colebrook) for turbulent flow.
assumptions: Fully developed flow in a straight pipe of constant diameter
f depends on Re and relative roughness ε/D
Fittings and valves add minor losses K v^{2}/(2g)

example.problem: Water flows at 2 m/s through 50 m of 50 mm pipe with f = 0.02. Find the head loss and pressure drop.

dB/dt = d/dt ∫_{CV} ρb dV + ∫_{CS} ρb (v.title: Reynolds transport theorem
dB/dt = d/dt ∫_{CV} ρb dV + ∫_{CS} ρb (v.about: Converts a conservation law written for a fixed mass of material (a system) into one for a fixed region of space (a control volume). The rate of change of a property B of the system equals its rate of change inside the CV plus its net outflow through the surface.
assumptions: Fixed, non-deforming control volume (for a moving CV use the relative velocity in the flux term)
B is extensive (mass, momentum, energy); b = dB/dm is the same quantity per unit mass
n is the outward unit normal, so v · n > 0 for outflow
vars: outward unit normal on the control surface

example.problem: A tank holds water, with 3 kg/s flowing in and 2 kg/s flowing out. Use the theorem with B = mass (b = 1) to find how fast the stored mass changes.

0 = d/dt ∫_{CV} ρ dV + ∫_{CS} ρ (v · n).title: Conservation of mass for a control volume
0 = d/dt ∫_{CV} ρ dV + ∫_{CS} ρ (v · n).about: Mass is neither created nor destroyed: the mass inside a control volume changes only by the net flow in through its surface. In steady flow, mass in equals mass out.
assumptions: Fixed control volume; v · n positive for outflow
No nuclear reactions (mass conserved)
related: steady, one in and one out

example.problem: A 1.2 m diameter tank is filled by a 50 mm pipe at 3 m/s while it drains at 2 L/s. How fast does the level rise?

Σ F = d/dt ∫_{CV} ρv dV + ∫_{CS} ρv (v ·.title: Linear momentum equation for a control volume
Σ F = d/dt ∫_{CV} ρv dV + ∫_{CS} ρv (v ·.about: Newton's second law for a control volume: the net external force equals the rate of change of momentum stored inside plus the net momentum flowing out. Use it for forces on pipe bends, nozzles, jets and vanes.
assumptions: Inertial (non-accelerating) control volume
ΣF includes pressure forces on the control surface, body forces such as gravity, and support forces
It is a vector equation: write each component separately
vars: net external force on the CV contents
related: steady, one in and one out
force of a jet stopped by a flat plate

example.problem: A water jet 30 mm in diameter at 20 m/s hits a flat plate head-on and spreads sideways. Find the force on the plate.
steps: Steady; x momentum in is ṁv, out is 0: F_{x} = ṁ(0 − 20) = −283 N on the water
The plate feels 283 N in the jet direction

Σ M = d/dt ∫_{CV} ρ(r × v) dV + ∫_{CS} ρ.title: Angular momentum equation for a control volume
Σ M = d/dt ∫_{CV} ρ(r × v) dV + ∫_{CS} ρ.about: The net torque on a control volume equals the rate of change of angular momentum inside plus its net outflow: Newton's second law for rotation applied to a fixed region that fluid passes through. It gives the torque on pumps, turbines and lawn sprinklers (Euler's turbomachine equation).
assumptions: Inertial control volume; r measured from a fixed point
Torques from surface forces, body forces and shafts all count in Σ τ
Only the tangential velocity v_{θ} contributes to the axial torque; the radial part does not
vars: position vector from the reference point

example.problem: A centrifugal pump impeller handles 0.05 m^{3}/s of water. Flow enters with no swirl and leaves at r_{2} = 0.15 m with tangential velocity 20 m/s. Find the shaft torque.

Σ M = d/dt ∫_{CV} ρ(r × v) dV + ∫_{CS} ρ.try: 50 kg/s * 0.15 m * 20 m/s to N m

Q̇ − Ẇ = d/dt ∫_{CV} ρe dV + ∫_{CS} ρ(e.title: Energy equation for a control volume (first law)
Q̇ − Ẇ = d/dt ∫_{CV} ρe dV + ∫_{CS} ρ(e.about: Heat added minus work done by the CV equals the rate of change of stored energy plus the net energy carried out by the flow. The p/ρ term is flow work, which combines with internal energy to make enthalpy.
assumptions: Ẇ is shaft and other work, not flow work (that is in p/ρ)
e = u + v^{2}/2 + gz per unit mass
Fixed control volume; signs: Q̇ into the CV positive, Ẇ by the CV positive
vars: heat transfer rate into the CV
work rate done by the CV (shaft, shear)
energy per unit mass, u + v^{2}/2 + gz
related: steady, one in and one out

example.problem: A 200 L insulated tank of water (no flow) is stirred by a 500 W mixer. How fast does its temperature rise? (c = 4186 J/(kg·K))
steps: No flow: dE_{CV}/dt = Q̇ − Ẇ = 0 − (−500) = 500 W
m c dT/dt = 500, with m = 200 kg

ṁ = ρ_{1} A_{1} v_{1} = ρ_{2} A_{2} v_{2.title: Continuity: steady mass flow through a duct
ṁ = ρ_{1} A_{1} v_{1} = ρ_{2} A_{2} v_{2.about: In steady flow with one inlet and one outlet, the mass flow rate is the same at both. For a liquid (constant ρ), A_{1}v_{1} = A_{2}v_{2}, so the fluid speeds up where the duct narrows.
assumptions: Steady flow, one inlet and one outlet
Uniform velocity and density across each section (use mean values)
v normal to A

example.problem: Air at 1.2 kg/m^{3} enters a 0.5 m^{2} duct at 8 m/s and leaves through 0.2 m^{2} at 1.0 kg/m^{3}. Find ṁ and the exit velocity.

Σ F = ṁ (v_{2} − v_{1}).title: Steady-flow momentum equation, one inlet and one outlet
Σ F = ṁ (v_{2} − v_{1}).about: In steady flow the net force on the fluid in a control volume equals the mass flow rate times its change in velocity. Use vectors: a pipe bend with no change in speed still needs a force to turn the flow.
assumptions: Steady, one inlet and one outlet, uniform velocity at each
ΣF includes pressure forces p_{1}A_{1} and p_{2}A_{2} at the cuts, weight, and the support force
Vector equation: apply in x and y separately
vars: net external force on the fluid in the CV

example.problem: A 90° bend carries 20 kg/s of water at 4 m/s, pressure effects neglected. Find the force the bend exerts on the water.

Q̇ − Ẇ = ṁ (h_{2} − h_{1} + (v_{2}^{2} −.title: Steady-flow energy equation
Q̇ − Ẇ = ṁ (h_{2} − h_{1} + (v_{2}^{2} −.about: The first law for steady devices with one inlet and one outlet: turbines, compressors, pumps, nozzles, heat exchangers and throttles. Heat in minus work out equals the mass flow times the change in enthalpy, kinetic and potential energy.
assumptions: Steady flow, one inlet and one outlet
Uniform properties across each section
Ẇ is shaft work done by the fluid (positive for a turbine, negative for a pump)
Kinetic and potential terms are often negligible except in nozzles and diffusers
vars: heat transfer rate into the fluid

example.problem: Steam enters an adiabatic turbine at 3 kg/s with h_{1} = 3230 kJ/kg and leaves with h_{2} = 2400 kJ/kg; velocity and height changes are small. Find the power.

∂ρ/∂t + ∇ · (ρv) = 0.title: Continuity equation at a point
∂ρ/∂t + ∇ · (ρv) = 0.about: Conservation of mass for an infinitesimal volume: density at a point rises only if more mass flows in than out. For incompressible flow it reduces to ∇ · v = 0, a constraint every velocity field must satisfy.
assumptions: Continuum; ρ and v differentiable
No sources or sinks of mass
related: 0 = d/dt ∫_{CV} ρ dV + ∫_{CS} ρ (v · n) dA

example.problem: An incompressible 2D flow has u = 3x (1/s). Find the y velocity v if v = 0 on y = 0, and evaluate it at y = 2 m.
steps: v = −3y, so at y = 2 m: v = −6 m/s

ρ Dv/Dt = −∇p + μ∇^{2}v + ρg.title: Navier–Stokes equations (incompressible)
ρ Dv/Dt = −∇p + μ∇^{2}v + ρg.about: Newton's second law for a Newtonian fluid: mass times acceleration equals pressure force plus viscous force plus gravity, per unit volume. With continuity (∇ · v = 0) it governs almost all fluid flow; only simple cases have exact solutions.
assumptions: Newtonian fluid with constant viscosity μ
Incompressible, constant density
Dv/Dt = ∂v/∂t + (v · ∇)v is the material (following-the-particle) acceleration, which makes the equation nonlinear
related: Euler equation, which integrates to Bernoulli

example.problem: Steady laminar flow between fixed parallel plates 2 mm apart: oil with μ = 0.05 Pa·s, pressure gradient dp/dx = −2 kPa/m. Find the centreline velocity.
steps: Steady and fully developed, so Dv/Dt = 0 and 0 = −dp/dx + μ d^{2}u/dy^{2}
With u = 0 at y = ±h, h = 1 mm: u = (−dp/dx)(h^{2} − y^{2})/(2μ)

ρ Dv/Dt = −∇p + μ∇^{2}v + ρg.try: 2 kPa/m * (1 mm)^2 / (2 * 0.05 Pa s) to mm/s

R = √(((σ_{x} − σ_{y})/2)^{2} + τ_{xy}^{.title: Mohr's circle radius
R = √(((σ_{x} − σ_{y})/2)^{2} + τ_{xy}^{.about: Mohr's circle for plane stress is centred at C = (σ_{x} + σ_{y})/2 on the σ axis with this radius. The principal stresses are C ± R and the largest in-plane shear stress equals R. Plot the points (σ_{x}, τ_{xy}) and (σ_{y}, −τ_{xy}); they lie at the ends of a diameter.
assumptions: Plane stress (σ_{z} = τ_{xz} = τ_{yz} = 0)

example.problem: A point has σ_{x} = 80 MPa, σ_{y} = −20 MPa, τ_{xy} = 30 MPa. Find Mohr's circle and the principal stresses.

σ = P/A ± Mc/I.title: Combined loading: axial plus bending stress
σ = P/A ± Mc/I.about: A member that carries an axial force and a bending moment at once has the two normal stresses added by superposition: the uniform P/A plus the bending stress, which is tensile on one face and compressive on the other. An eccentric load P at offset e is the same with M = P e.
assumptions: Linear elastic, small deflections, so stresses superpose
c is the distance from the neutral axis to the face; take the sign that matches each face
vars: distance from neutral axis to the face

example.problem: A 50 mm wide, 100 mm deep bar carries 20 kN of tension and a 3 kN·m bending moment. Find the largest and smallest stress.

ȳ = (Σ A_{i} y_{i})/(Σ A_{i}).title: Neutral axis: centroid of a composite section
ȳ = (Σ A_{i} y_{i})/(Σ A_{i}).about: In bending, the neutral axis passes through the centroid of the cross-section. For a T, I or built-up section split it into rectangles, take each area times its own centroid height, and divide by the total area. Then find I about that axis with the parallel-axis theorem.
assumptions: Homogeneous material
y_{i} measured from one reference line, often the bottom

example.problem: A T-section has a 100 × 20 mm flange on top of a 20 mm wide, 80 mm tall web. Where is the neutral axis, from the bottom?
steps: web: A = 1600 mm^{2}, y = 40 mm; flange: A = 2000 mm^{2}, y = 90 mm

ρ = m/V.title: Density: mass per volume
ρ = m/V.about: Density says how much mass fills a unit of volume. It is the starting property of every fluid problem: it turns volumes into masses, flow rates into mass flow rates and depths into pressures.
assumptions: Uniform fluid, or an average over the volume
Liquids barely change density with pressure; gases follow p = ρRT

example.problem: A 2.5 L jug of liquid has a mass of 3.15 kg. Find its density.

γ = W/V = ρg.title: Specific weight: weight per volume
γ = W/V = ρg.about: Specific weight is the weight of a unit volume of fluid, density times g. It appears wherever gravity acts on a fluid: hydrostatic pressure p = γh, buoyancy and the energy equation written in heads.
assumptions: g constant, 9.81 m/s^{2} at the Earth's surface
Water at 4 °C: γ = 9.81 kN/m^{3}
related: pressure grows by γ per metre of depth

example.problem: Find the specific weight of seawater, ρ = 1025 kg/m^{3}.

SG = ρ/ρ_{w} = γ/γ_{w}.title: Specific gravity
SG = ρ/ρ_{w} = γ/γ_{w}.about: Specific gravity compares a fluid with water at 4 °C (ρ = 1000 kg/m^{3}). It has no units, so tables list it instead of density: multiply by 1000 kg/m^{3} to get ρ.
assumptions: Reference is water at 4 °C, ρ_{w} = 1000 kg/m^{3}, γ_{w} = 9.81 kN/m^{3}
For gases, SG is sometimes taken against air instead: check the table

example.problem: Mercury has SG = 13.6. Find its density and specific weight.

ν = μ/ρ.title: Kinematic viscosity
ν = μ/ρ.about: Kinematic viscosity is dynamic viscosity divided by density. It is how fast momentum diffuses through the fluid, and it is what the Reynolds number really needs: Re = vD/ν.
assumptions: μ is the dynamic viscosity from τ = μ du/dy
Both μ and ν depend strongly on temperature

example.problem: Water at 20 °C has μ = 1.002 × 10^{−3} Pa·s and ρ = 998 kg/m^{3}. Find ν.

p = ρRT.title: Ideal gas law (density form)
p = ρRT.about: For a gas, density follows from pressure and temperature. Use it to find ρ for air before Bernoulli, drag or Reynolds number, and to see when a gas is compressible.
assumptions: p and T absolute: Pa and kelvin, never gage pressure or °C
R is the gas constant of that gas: 287 J/(kg·K) for air
related: when a gas may be treated as incompressible
with ρ = p/(RT) for the atmosphere

example.problem: Find the density of air at 101.3 kPa and 15 °C.

ρ = constant.title: Incompressible flow
ρ = constant.about: A fluid whose density does not change is incompressible. Liquids nearly always are, and gases are too when they move slower than about Mach 0.3, where density changes stay under about 5 %. It makes continuity A_{1}v_{1} = A_{2}v_{2} and Bernoulli's equation hold.
assumptions: Liquids: nearly always
Gases: Ma = v/c below about 0.3, and small temperature changes

example.problem: Air flows past a car at 30 m/s (c = 343 m/s). May it be treated as incompressible?

Ma = v/c.title: Mach number
Ma = v/c.about: The Mach number is flow speed over the speed of sound. It sorts gas flows: below about 0.3 density hardly changes, near 1 shocks can form.
assumptions: c = √(kRT) for an ideal gas, about 343 m/s in air at 20 °C

example.problem: An airliner cruises at 250 m/s where c = 295 m/s. Find its Mach number.

p_{abs} = p_{gage} + p_{atm}.title: Absolute and gage pressure
p_{abs} = p_{gage} + p_{atm}.about: Gauges read pressure above the atmosphere; absolute pressure counts from a vacuum. Use absolute pressure in the ideal gas law and gage pressure for forces on walls that have air on the other side.
assumptions: p_{atm} = 101.3 kPa at sea level; less at altitude
A vacuum reading is a negative gage pressure

example.problem: A tyre gauge reads 220 kPa at sea level. Find the absolute pressure.

y_{cp} = y_{c} + I_{xc}/(y_{c} A).title: Centre of pressure on a submerged flat plate
y_{cp} = y_{c} + I_{xc}/(y_{c} A).about: The resultant force on a submerged plate acts below its centroid, because pressure grows with depth. The extra distance is the second moment of area over y_{c} A, which shrinks as the plate goes deeper.
assumptions: Liquid at rest, constant density, free surface at gage pressure zero
y measured along the plate's slant from where its plane meets the free surface
I_{xc} about the horizontal axis through the centroid
vars: depth along the slant to the centre of pressure
second moment of area about the centroid

example.problem: A vertical gate 2 m wide and 3 m tall has its top at the water surface. Find the centre of pressure.
example.answer: y_{cp} = 2.0 m below the surface (two thirds down)

Q = A v.title: Volume flow rate
Q = A v.about: The volume flow rate is the area the fluid crosses times its average velocity, with the area taken perpendicular to the flow. It is the quantity pumps, pipes and continuity are written in.
assumptions: A is perpendicular to the velocity; v is uniform across A or is its average
For a slanted area use the velocity component normal to it

example.problem: Water moves at 2 m/s in a 50 mm diameter pipe. Find Q.

ṁ = ρQ = ρ A v.title: Mass flow rate
ṁ = ρQ = ρ A v.about: Mass flow rate is mass crossing a section per second. Unlike Q it stays the same along a steady pipe even when density changes, so use it for gases and for the control-volume equations.
assumptions: Uniform density and velocity across A, or averages
Steady flow: the same ṁ enters and leaves

example.problem: Water (ρ = 1000 kg/m^{3}) flows at 3.93 L/s. Find ṁ.

ṁ = ∫_{A} ρ u dA.title: Mass flow rate for a non-uniform velocity
ṁ = ∫_{A} ρ u dA.about: When the velocity varies across a section, add up ρu over each small piece of area. In vector form this is ∫ ρ (v · n) dA: only the velocity component normal to the area carries fluid through it.
assumptions: u is the local velocity normal to the area
Same idea as the control-surface term in the mass balance
related: 0 = d/dt ∫_{CV} ρ dV + ∫_{CS} ρ (v · n) dA

example.problem: Water (ρ = 1000 kg/m^{3}) flows in a 20 mm radius pipe with u = 2(1 − r^{2}/R^{2}) m/s. Find ṁ.

ṁ = ∫_{A} ρ u dA.try: 1000 kg/m^3 * pi (20 mm)^2 * 1 m/s to kg/s

v = (1/A) ∫_{A} u dA.title: Average velocity
v = (1/A) ∫_{A} u dA.about: The average velocity is the uniform speed that would carry the same flow rate, Q/A. It is the v in Q = Av, Reynolds number and head-loss formulas.
assumptions: Incompressible, or density constant across the section
related: laminar pipe: the centre is twice the average

example.problem: In laminar pipe flow the centreline speed is 0.6 m/s. Find the average velocity.

u = v.title: Uniform velocity profile
u = v.about: Every bit of fluid crosses the section at the same speed, so the local velocity u equals the average v. It is the model for ideal (frictionless) flow and the usual assumption in Bernoulli and one-dimensional control-volume work.
assumptions: Viscous effects ignored, or the flow is outside a boundary layer
A good model for turbulent pipe flow, whose profile is fairly flat
related: real laminar pipe flow, no slip at the wall

example.problem: A uniform 1.5 m/s stream crosses a 0.2 m^{2} opening. Find Q.

u = 2v (1 − r^{2}/R^{2}).title: Laminar pipe flow: the parabolic profile
u = 2v (1 − r^{2}/R^{2}).about: Fluid sticks to the wall (no slip), so the velocity grows from zero at the wall to a maximum at the centre. Once the boundary layers from the walls meet, past the entrance length, the laminar profile is a parabola whose centre speed is twice the average.
assumptions: Laminar (Re below about 2300), steady, incompressible, Newtonian
Fully developed: past the entrance length L_{e}
Round pipe of radius R
related: Poiseuille: the flow this profile carries

example.problem: Oil flows with average velocity 0.4 m/s in a 30 mm pipe, laminar. Find the speed 10 mm from the centre.

L_{e}/D ≈ 0.06 Re.title: Entrance length, laminar
L_{e}/D ≈ 0.06 Re.about: Near a pipe inlet the velocity profile is still changing as the wall boundary layers grow. In laminar flow they meet after about 0.06 Re diameters; beyond that the profile is the fully developed parabola.
assumptions: Laminar, Re below about 2300
Roughly uniform flow at the inlet

δ ≈ 5x/√(Re_{x}).title: Laminar boundary layer thickness (Blasius)
δ ≈ 5x/√(Re_{x}).about: Over a flat plate, fluid at the wall is at rest and a thin layer of slowed fluid grows downstream; outside it the flow is the free stream U_{∞}. Inside this boundary layer viscosity matters; outside it the flow is nearly frictionless. δ is where u reaches 99 % of U_{∞}.
assumptions: Laminar: Re_{x} below about 5 × 10^{5}
Flat plate at zero angle, no pressure gradient
x measured from the leading edge

Re_{x} = ρU_{∞}x/μ.title: Local Reynolds number on a plate
Re_{x} = ρU_{∞}x/μ.about: The Reynolds number built on the distance from the leading edge. It grows downstream; the boundary layer turns turbulent at about 5 × 10^{5}.
assumptions: U_{∞} is the free-stream speed outside the boundary layer
Transition near 5 × 10^{5} on a smooth plate; earlier if rough or disturbed

v = √(2(p_{0} − p)/ρ).title: Pitot tube: speed from a pressure difference
v = √(2(p_{0} − p)/ρ).about: A Pitot tube brings the flow to rest at its tip, where the pressure rises to the stagnation pressure p_{0}. Bernoulli between the free stream and the tip turns the difference p_{0} − p into the speed.
assumptions: Steady, incompressible, frictionless along the streamline into the tip
p is the static pressure of the stream, p_{0} the stagnation pressure at the tip
Airspeed below about Mach 0.3

example.problem: A Pitot-static probe in air (ρ = 1.225 kg/m^{3}) reads p_{0} − p = 600 Pa. Find the airspeed.
